lesson.title: Read the Fine Print: When the Standard Deviation Formula Actually Applies
lesson.summary: The formula for the standard deviation of p-hat is only accurate when the sample is a small fraction of the population and when the sample is large enough for successes and failures to both be well represented, two conditions known as the 10 percent condition and the large counts condition.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter ended with a mismatch: the formula square root of p(1-p)/n predicted a standard deviation of about 0.346 for the marble example, but the exact enumeration gave 0.3. That gap exists because the formula assumes something the marble example violated. The formula for the standard deviation of p-hat is derived assuming each observation in the sample is essentially independent of the others, the way it would be if you sampled with replacement, or equivalently, sampled from an infinitely large population. In the marble example, the population had only five marbles, and the sample took two of them, fully 40 percent of the entire population, without replacement. Once you remove a red marble from a population of five, the odds for the next draw change noticeably, so the draws are not independent, and the formula's assumption breaks down.

This gives the first condition: the 10 percent condition. The formula square root of p(1-p)/n is safe to use only when the sample size n is no more than 10 percent of the population size N. When a sample is a small slice of a much larger population, removing sampled individuals barely changes the odds for those remaining, so treating the draws as approximately independent is a reasonable approximation, even though technically sampling is done without replacement. When the sample is a large slice of a small population, as in the marble example, that approximation fails, and the true standard deviation can differ meaningfully from what the formula predicts. As a technical note for the curious, the marble example's exact standard deviation of 0.3 can be recovered from the formula's 0.346 by multiplying by a finite population correction factor, the square root of (N-n)/(N-1), which here is the square root of 3/4, approximately 0.866, and 0.346 times 0.866 is indeed 0.3. That correction is a good check on the formula, but it is not something you are expected to compute routinely, the 10 percent condition exists so you can usually ignore it.

The second condition is the large counts condition, and it addresses a different concern: whether the sampling distribution of p-hat is shaped closely enough to a normal curve for the mean and standard deviation to be genuinely useful for probability calculations. The large counts condition requires both np and n(1-p) to be at least 10, where p is the population proportion, or the best available estimate of it. This ensures the sample is expected to contain a reasonable number of both successes and failures, not so few of one category that the distribution is lopsided or lumpy near a boundary at 0 or 1.

Consider a case where this condition fails. Suppose p = 0.4 but the sample size is only n = 20. Then np = (20)(0.4) = 8, which is less than 10, so the large counts condition is not met, even though n(1-p) = (20)(0.6) = 12 clears the bar on its own. Because both parts must hold, this sample fails the condition overall, and the sampling distribution of p-hat would be noticeably skewed rather than bell-shaped, since with an expected count of only 8 successes, it is quite possible to see 3 or 4, but essentially impossible to see negative successes, creating a lopsided distribution near the low end. Compare that to a sample of n = 50 with the same p = 0.4: np = 20 and n(1-p) = 30, both comfortably above 10, and the large counts condition is satisfied. In practice, both the 10 percent condition and the large counts condition need to hold before you trust the formula from the previous chapter, or before you use a normal curve to compute probabilities involving p-hat.
